initialNumericalReport.program: Home safety, accessibility and critical repairs

what: Rebuilding Together Metro Chicago repairs homes for low-income residents, with priority for older and disabled homeowners.
Its safety and accessibility work includes handrails, grab bars and other critical repairs.
Volunteer teams, skilled trades, sponsors and public partners help residents remain in their homes.
strengths: Home hazards and accessibility barriers are concrete, actionable needs.
Local repair delivery and completed county projects demonstrate an operating mechanism.
Targeted repairs can protect both safety and household resources.
reservations: Completed repairs do not establish additional falls or serious injuries prevented.
Recognized in-kind costs and public funding complicate the return to an ordinary gift.
Actual avoided spending, disruptions, displacement and full portfolio effects remain uncertain.

sections.what: Rebuilding Together Metro Chicago, EIN 36-3803312, is the independent recipient for free repairs and accessibility improvements in Chicago and Cook County. Safe at Home includes grab bars, handrails and smoke detectors; other programs provide larger home repairs and nonprofit facility work. The official donation page identifies a registered nonprofit and current giving route, but no transaction was tested. Native delivery is repaired homes, not volunteer attendance or headquarters location.
sections.monitoring: The county confirms 30 veteran-owned homes repaired with $1.25 million of previously allocated ARPA funding, completed by May 2025. Those homes are baseline, not a new gift's entire output. Cumulative homes since 1991 and claimed service-value multipliers do not establish current incremental health or cash. Track completed additional homes, selected high-risk residents, actual hazard removal, falls, injuries, repair disruptions, money otherwise spent and alternative programs. Observe durability and maintenance rather than assuming permanent benefit.
sections.qualitative: The 2023 Cochrane review finds high-certainty fall-rate reductions from targeted home hazard interventions in higher-risk older adults; the .62 rate ratio is external, not a local RTMC effect. It searched through January 2021, usually followed people for one year and provides little evidence on serious injury prevention. Independence-focused modifications are not automatically the same tested intervention. The model therefore uses explicit high-risk selection and .5 local transport attenuation. Average acute QALY area per avoided fall is a separate weak judgment, not a claim that every fall causes a fracture or death. No mortality or ordinary survivor earnings are priced. The review does not clearly establish reductions in fractures, hospitalization or medically attended falls, and finds little important quality-of-life change. Thus .01 QALY per avoided fall remains a weak acute-area hypothesis under uncertain/null injury endpoints; the fall-rate evidence alone cannot validate that area.
sections.cost:
FY2025 tax expense is $2,993,738. Original Schedule D removes $278,560 donated services/use of facilities from audited expenses; adding that recognized in-kind expense gives $3,272,298 full annual cost. Direct event expense is zero and no rental addback was identified. Comparable full FY2024 and FY2023 costs are $2,248,873 and $2,085,610 after adding $243,542 and $290,830 donated-service expense. Mean full recognized annual cost is $2,535,593.67. This consistent accounting basis includes recognized in-kind resources; additional unrecognized volunteer opportunity costs remain unknown and are not arbitrarily valued by a retail service multiplier.

A judged 100 local household repair opportunities and .5 additional annual-work response imply 50 exposed households. Thirty contain one modeled higher-risk older resident. A judged one fall per person-year, external .62 fall-rate ratio and .5 local transport factor imply 5.7 avoided falls over one finite year. The .01 expected acute QALY per avoided fall averages across minor and serious outcomes, including falls with no injury; it is a judgment, not a proven fracture reduction. After a half-year delay at 3%, the result is .056164 clinical QALYs. No additional accessibility utility is stacked on the same residents.

Twenty households have a judged $500 one-year net energy/care-resource gain and $1,000 one-time spending they would actually otherwise pay within that year. Each positive component retains .5 for health overlap before the full $100 disruption/time/care burden is subtracted, leaving $650. Thirty other households lose $100. All gains exclude taxes, benefit withdrawal, new maintenance costs, replacement resources and displaced earnings; the separate $100 is temporary repair disruption rather than repeated maintenance. Retail donated repair value, property appreciation and gross salary are excluded. Actual alternative spending is a required conditional premise, not an observed household fact.

At $25,000 annual resources, one welfareperson per household and one finite year, a joint log gives .5 × [20 log(1 + 650/25,000) + 30 log(1 − 100/25,000)] / 1.03^.5 = .193674 equivalents. Together .249837 implies $130.977170 million per ten combined equivalents, not ten clinical QALYs. Clinical residents are a subset of all resource-exposed repair households; changed and unchanged financial branches are disjoint, with a 50-household union for full harm stress. Resource exposure and disruption remain when health fails.

Positive overlap never shrinks negative components or costs. Distinct local contractor/payer losses and external care burdens are explicit stresses; recognized donated expense is not counted again as a household opportunity burden. Central counterparty incidence is unknown-neutral, not factual zero or complete-world benefit. Public opportunity costs, nonlocal incidence, displacement and the broader portfolio remain unknown.
sections.funding: FY2025 original government grants are $1,865,647. Current repairs rely on public programs, sponsors and volunteer resources; completed ARPA-funded work and available alternatives stay in the counterfactual. Large repair amounts are not automatically household income gains, and operating recipient costs are not a marginal cash need. The .5 response prior judges additional annual funded work while retaining the full annual denominator; b=1 shows full response. No specific unfunded donor expansion or funding replacement rate was established. A secondary audit-control lead is not asserted as an original verified finding in this bounded phase.

model.costScope: FY2025 tax expense is $2,993,738. Original Schedule D removes $278,560 donated services/use of facilities from audited expenses; adding that recognized in-kind expense gives $3,272,298 full annual cost. Direct event expense is zero and no rental addback was identified. Comparable full FY2024 and FY2023 costs are $2,248,873 and $2,085,610 after adding $243,542 and $290,830 donated-service expense. model.geographicAttribution: Chicago/Cook repair households; one high-risk clinical resident within resource-exposed household subset.
model.formula: exposed=N*b; clinicalPeople=exposed*highRisk; avoidedFalls=clinicalPeople*fallRate*(1−externalRR)*transport. Q=avoidedFalls*qPerFall*discounted finite years−full union harm. Signed energy/care and one-time actual spending components preserve full negatives, then net household costs before one log. Price=10*C/(health+resources).
model.counterfactual: Existing county-funded repairs, alternative providers, owner spending and sponsor/volunteer resources continue.
model.attribution: Additional annual response, household throughput, high-risk selection, transport, injury area and resource changes are distinct conditional judgments.
model.uncertainty: Full portfolio, serious-injury causality, actual household spending, unrecognized social costs and marginal gift effects unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional completed repaired homes, targeted avoided falls, finite expected acute injury burden and signed net household resources; no donated-value-as-income.
